title: He loved them to the end (John 13:1–17)
hook: he washes the feet of every disciple, even Judas

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus's last public words in John, with the urgency of sunset. Your line was while you have the light.

Sandals, dirt roads, donkeys and sheep. Arrive at a dinner in Jesus's world and your feet would be filthy. A host might offer water, and the washing was a servant's job. Now it's the evening before Passover. Jesus and his friends are already at supper, and the dust of the road is still on their feet. Nobody has washed anyone's feet. And John opens a new part of his Gospel with one sentence.

"Now before the feast of the passover, when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father, having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Unto the end can mean two things in Greek: to the last moment, and to the uttermost, completely. Both are true here. Then Jesus gets up from supper, takes off his outer robe, and ties a towel around his waist, dressed like a servant. "After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded." When he gets to Peter, Peter refuses: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." And Peter swings to the other extreme: "Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head." From never to everything, in two breaths. John doesn't hide one detail: the devil had already put it into Judas's heart to betray him. Jesus knows; he says, not all of you are clean. And he washes every disciple's feet anyway, including the feet that will walk out to betray him. Then, robed again, he says: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." Churches keep this command differently. Some Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches wash feet in the Holy Thursday service. Some Mennonite and Brethren churches wash feet regularly as an ordinance. Others hear it mainly as a call to humble service.
screen: `TO THE LAST, AND TO THE UTTERMOST.`
then, large: `HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who's hard for you, not dangerous, just difficult: a coworker who grates on you, a relative you avoid, someone who let you down. Picture yourself doing one small, humble thing for them, making their coffee, helping with a task, saying something kind about them to someone else, and let the resistance in you be there. If you pray, ask for the humility to serve them anyway; if not, just hold the picture.
Towel. What Jesus tied around his waist, dressed like a servant, before he knelt to wash every disciple's feet.
Your line: to the end. A towel, a basin, and every pair of feet. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Some churches wash feet on Holy Thursday, the evening before Good Friday; some Mennonite and Brethren churches practice footwashing regularly, and others keep the command through acts of humble service.

chat.says: Why did Jesus wash his friends' feet? Isn't that strange for a leader?
options: He took a servant's job out of love, and said: wash one another's feet too.
Because no servant came that night, and somebody simply had to do it.
He washed every disciple's feet except Judas's, knowing who'd betray him.
chat.meaning: He loved them unto the end: dressed like a servant, he washed every disciple's feet, even Judas's, and told them to wash one another's feet.

Holy Thursday.meaning: the Thursday before Easter, when some churches wash feet

Mennonite.meaning: a Christian tradition where some churches wash feet as an ordinance

ordinance.meaning: a practice a church keeps regularly as Jesus's command

Judas.meaning: the disciple who would betray Jesus

notes: Footwashing practices: Holy Thursday (Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, others); ordinance in many Mennonite, Brethren, some Baptist and Adventist churches. Confirm.
'Usually the lowest servant': footwashing by slaves; confirm generalization (cf. 1 Samuel 25:41).
The text implies Judas's feet were washed (13:2, 10–11) without stating it outright; confirm phrasing.
KJV 'bason' is the 1769 spelling; inside quotation.
